abstract: The ILO's biennial Global Employment Trends for Youth, 2026 edition, published 2026-08-11. Its contribution to jobsdata.ai is the first global sizing of youth-specific AI exposure: 6.1 per cent of the 913.8 million jobs held by people aged 15 to 29 worldwide fall in the ILO's most-exposed occupational gradients, about 55.8 million jobs, and an illustrative scenario in which a tenth of those disappear implies 5.6 million youth transitions. The more useful number for a US-focused dashboard is the regional split: Northern America sits at 14.3 per cent youth exposure against 1.3 per cent in sub-Saharan Africa, a more than tenfold gap that tracks income level almost perfectly. ILO frames that gap in both directions - low exposure means less replacement risk but also foregone productivity gain.
keyFindings: Global sizing: 'The report estimates that 6.1 per cent of jobs currently held by young people aged 15 to 29 fall in the categories of those most exposed to AI' - 55.8 million of 913.8 million youth jobs, using gradients 3 and 4 of the ILO occupational exposure scale, predominantly clerical and support work.

Illustrative disappearance scenario: 'If only 10 per cent of the jobs that are exposed to AI disappear in full, that would translate into 5.6 million employed youth at the global level either facing unemployment, shifting into another job or exiting the labour force.'
Regional decomposition of that 5.6 million: Eastern Asia 1.5 million, Latin America and the Caribbean 785,000, South-Eastern Asia and the Pacific 716,000, Northern America 618,000.

Exposure tracks national income almost linearly: 'High-income and upper-middle-income countries have considerably higher AI exposure risks for youth (14.3 and 7.6 per cent, respectively, compared to 3.1 per cent in lower-middle-income countries and 0.9 per cent in low-income countries).'

Subregional ranking: Northern, Southern and Western Europe highest at 14.9 per cent, Northern America 14.3, Eastern Europe 12.8; lowest are the Arab States 5.8, Northern Africa 4.0, Southern Asia 2.8, sub-Saharan Africa 1.3.

ILO explicitly resists reading low exposure as an advantage: in low-proliferation regions a worker's job 'is less at risk of AI replacement, but negative in the sense that the worker potentially misses out on the productivity gain.'

The report is repeatedly hedged on causation: 'the degree to which risk translates to job loss is still debatable.' Exposure here is a capability-overlap classification, not an observed displacement count.
methodology: Applies the ILO's occupational AI exposure gradient scale (a four-level classification of ISCO occupations by the share of tasks amenable to generative AI, developed in ILO's earlier GenAI exposure work) to harmonised global employment estimates for the 15-29 age band, drawn from the ILO modelled estimates database. Exposure shares are computed as the youth employment weight in gradients 3 and 4. The 5.6 million figure is not an estimate or forecast - it is an arithmetic scenario, 10 per cent of the exposed stock, chosen for illustration and labelled as such. No microdata, no firm-level observation, and no post-ChatGPT employment change is measured anywhere in the AI section.
qualifiers: Tier 1 institutional statistics, but the AI content is exposure classification rather than measurement, and the headline transition figure is an assumption multiplied by a stock. Two hard gates keep it out of the plotted series on jobsdata.ai: population (15-29 globally, not ages 22-25 in the US) and geography (the 14.3 per cent Northern America figure pools the US and Canada). The exposure gradients are occupation-level and predate current agentic capability, so they will mismeasure both directions. Most importantly, the income gradient in exposure is largely a composition artefact - rich countries have more clerical and professional employment - so it describes where exposed occupations exist, not where displacement is occurring. Do not treat the 6.1 per cent or 14.3 per cent as displacement forecasts, and do not compare the 5.6 million against modelled displacement projections such as Goldman's 15 million, which are constructed on entirely different logic.
